decks.title: Electric Charges and Fields — Part 1: Charge, Coulomb’s law and the electric field
goals: State the basic properties of electric charge and explain charging by induction
Apply Coulomb’s law in vector form and the principle of superposition
Calculate the electric field of a point charge and of a system of charges
Sketch and interpret electric field-line patterns

slides.heading: Electric Charges and Fields
slides.body_md: Part 1 — what charge is, how charges push and pull, and how the idea of a **field** describes that push and pull at every point in space.

visual.alt: Flow of the part: charge, Coulomb force, superposition, electric field, field lines

slides.narration: Pull off a woollen sweater on a dry winter evening in Delhi and you hear crackles and may even see sparks. That is electrostatics at work. In this part we describe charge, find the force between charges with Coulomb’s law, add forces from many charges, and then replace the force picture with the idea of an electric field that exists at every point around a charge.

slides.heading: Properties of electric charge
slides.body_md: Charge is a basic property of matter, measured in **coulombs (C)**. Four properties matter for every problem in this chapter.

rows: Positive and negative; like repel, unlike attract
Glass rubbed with silk is positive; the silk is negative
Total charge is the algebraic sum
Charge is neither created nor destroyed in an isolated system
$q = n e$, with $n$ an integer and $e = 1.6 \times 10^{-19}$ C

visual.alt: Table of the four basic properties of charge: two kinds, additivity, conservation and quantisation, with an example of each

slides.narration: There are two kinds of charge. Like charges repel and unlike charges attract. Charges add like ordinary numbers with signs, so a body with three positive and five negative units has two negative units in total. Charge is conserved: rubbing a rod only moves electrons from one body to the other. And charge comes in whole-number multiples of the electronic charge, which is about one point six times ten to the minus nineteen coulomb.

slides.heading: Quantisation in practice
slides.body_md: Since $q = n e$, the number of electrons transferred is $n = q/e$. A body charged to $-1.0\,\mu\text{C}$ has gained $n = \dfrac{1.0 \times 10^{-6}}{1.6 \times 10^{-19}} = 6.25 \times 10^{12}$ extra electrons.
bullets: Everyday charges are huge multiples of $e$, so charge looks continuous at the large scale.
A positively charged body has **lost** electrons; its mass decreases very slightly.
Quantisation matters at the atomic scale, for example in Millikan-style oil-drop experiments.

visual.alt: Table of three charges and the number of electrons gained or lost: minus one microcoulomb is six point two five times ten to the twelve electrons gained

slides.narration: To find how many electrons moved, divide the charge by the electronic charge. A body at minus one microcoulomb has gained more than six million million electrons. Numbers this large are why charge seems continuous in daily life. Remember the direction too: a positive body has lost electrons, a negative body has gained them. Protons do not move when we charge solids by rubbing.

slides.heading: Charging by induction
slides.body_md: A charged rod can charge a neutral conductor **without touching it**. The induced charge is opposite in sign to the rod.

nodes.label: Bring a negative rod near a metal sphere
Electrons pushed to the far side; near side becomes positive
Earth the sphere: far-side electrons flow to earth
Remove the earth wire, then the rod
Sphere left positively charged, spread uniformly

visual.alt: Five steps of charging a metal sphere by induction with a negative rod, ending with a positively charged sphere

slides.narration: Bring a negatively charged rod close to an insulated metal sphere. The free electrons in the sphere are pushed to the far side, so the near side is left positive. Now connect the far side to earth: electrons flow away to the ground. Break the earth connection first, and only then take the rod away. The sphere keeps a positive charge, which spreads evenly over its surface. The order of the last two steps matters.

slides.heading: Quick check: quantisation
slides.body_md: Which of these could be the charge on an oil drop?
slides.narration: Use quantisation. A possible charge must be a whole-number multiple of one point six times ten to the minus nineteen coulomb. Divide each option by that value and see which gives a whole number.

slides.heading: Coulomb’s law
slides.body_md:
The force between two point charges $q_1$ and $q_2$ a distance $r$ apart in vacuum acts along the line joining them and has magnitude
$$F = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\,\dfrac{|q_1 q_2|}{r^2} = k\,\dfrac{|q_1 q_2|}{r^2},\qquad k = 9 \times 10^{9}\ \text{N m}^2\,\text{C}^{-2}$$
bullets: $\varepsilon_0 = 8.85 \times 10^{-12}\ \text{C}^2\,\text{N}^{-1}\,\text{m}^{-2}$ is the permittivity of free space.
The forces on the two charges are equal and opposite (Newton’s third law).
Double the distance and the force becomes one quarter.

slides.narration: Coulomb found that the force between two small charged bodies is proportional to the product of the charges and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them. The constant k is about nine times ten to the nine in SI units. The force acts along the line joining the charges, repulsive for like charges and attractive for unlike ones. Each charge pulls or pushes the other with the same size of force.

slides.heading: Coulomb’s law in vector form and in a medium
slides.body_md: Directions matter, so write the law as a vector.
columns:
**Vector form**

Force on $q_2$ due to $q_1$:
$$\vec F_{21} = k\,\dfrac{q_1 q_2}{r^2}\,\hat r_{12}$$
where $\hat r_{12}$ is the unit vector **from $q_1$ to $q_2$**. If $q_1 q_2 > 0$ the force on $q_2$ points away from $q_1$ (repulsion); if $q_1 q_2 < 0$ it points towards $q_1$. Also $\vec F_{12} = -\vec F_{21}$.

**In a medium**

In a medium of permittivity $\varepsilon = \varepsilon_0 \varepsilon_r$ (dielectric constant $\varepsilon_r$):
$$F_\text{medium} = \dfrac{F_\text{vacuum}}{\varepsilon_r}$$
Water has $\varepsilon_r \approx 80$, so ionic forces in water are about 80 times weaker — one reason salt dissolves.

visual.alt: Table of dielectric constants: vacuum 1, glass 5 to 10, water 80, and how much the force is reduced

slides.narration: In vector form, the force on charge two points along the unit vector from charge one to charge two, multiplied by the product of the charges with their signs. A positive product gives repulsion and a negative product gives attraction, automatically. In a material medium the force is smaller by the dielectric constant. Water reduces the force about eighty times, which helps it pull salt crystals apart.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: force between two charges
slides.body_md: Two small spheres carry $+3.0\,\mu\text{C}$ and $-5.0\,\mu\text{C}$ and are $15$ cm apart in air. Find the force between them. What is it if the distance is doubled?
bullets: Step 2 — $F = \dfrac{9 \times 10^{9} \times 3.0 \times 10^{-6} \times 5.0 \times 10^{-6}}{0.15^2} = 6.0$ N.
Step 3 — unlike charges, so the force is **attractive**, along the line joining them.
Step 4 — doubling $r$ divides $F$ by 4: $F' = 1.5$ N.

visual.alt: Worked table: the product of charges, r squared, the force of six newtons and one point five newtons at double the distance

slides.narration: Convert microcoulombs and centimetres to SI units first; this is where most marks are lost. Put the magnitudes into Coulomb’s law and get six newtons, a large force for such small charges. The signs tell you the direction: unlike charges attract. Doubling the distance makes the force a quarter, so one and a half newtons. Always state the direction as well as the size.

slides.heading: Quick check: changing distance and charge
slides.body_md: Both charges are doubled and the distance between them is also doubled. What happens to the force?
slides.narration: Think in ratios. Doubling both charges multiplies the product of the charges by four. Doubling the distance divides the force by four. Combine the two effects.

slides.heading: Superposition of forces
slides.body_md:
The force on a charge due to several others is the **vector sum** of the forces due to each one acting alone:
$$\vec F_0 = \vec F_{01} + \vec F_{02} + \dots + \vec F_{0n}$$
Each pair force follows Coulomb’s law and is unaffected by the other charges.

slides.narration: When many charges act on one charge, work out each force separately as if the others were not there. Then add the forces as vectors, not as plain numbers. In the diagram, one force acts straight down and the other acts to the right, so the resultant is the diagonal of the rectangle they make. This principle of superposition is the key to every multi-charge problem.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: resultant force on a charge
slides.body_md: $q_0 = +1.0\,\mu\text{C}$ is at O. $q_1 = +4.0\,\mu\text{C}$ is $0.30$ m above O and $q_2 = -3.0\,\mu\text{C}$ is $0.30$ m to the right of O. Find the net force on $q_0$.
bullets: Step 1 — due to $q_1$ (repulsion, downwards): $F_1 = \dfrac{9 \times 10^{9} \times 4.0 \times 10^{-6} \times 1.0 \times 10^{-6}}{0.30^2} = 0.40$ N.
Step 2 — due to $q_2$ (attraction, to the right): $F_2 = \dfrac{9 \times 10^{9} \times 3.0 \times 10^{-6} \times 1.0 \times 10^{-6}}{0.30^2} = 0.30$ N.
Step 3 — perpendicular, so $F = \sqrt{0.40^2 + 0.30^2} = 0.50$ N.
Step 4 — direction: $\tan\theta = 0.40/0.30$, so $\theta \approx 53^\circ$ below the line from O towards $q_2$.

slides.narration: Find each force alone, with its direction from the signs. The four microcoulomb charge pushes the test charge downwards with zero point four newton. The negative charge pulls it to the right with zero point three newton. These two are at right angles, so use Pythagoras to get zero point five newton, and the tangent of the angle to get about fifty three degrees below the horizontal line.

slides.heading: The electric field
slides.body_md:
The **electric field** at a point is the force per unit positive test charge placed there:
$$\vec E = \lim_{q_0 \to 0}\dfrac{\vec F}{q_0}, \qquad \text{unit N C}^{-1}$$
For a point charge $q$: $\;\vec E = k\,\dfrac{q}{r^2}\,\hat r$, pointing away from $q$ if $q > 0$ and towards it if $q < 0$.
bullets: The test charge is kept tiny so it does not disturb the charges that produce the field.
Once $\vec E$ is known, the force on any charge $q$ placed there is $\vec F = q\vec E$.
A negative charge feels a force opposite to $\vec E$.

visual.alt: Radial field lines pointing outwards from a positive charge

slides.narration: Instead of asking what force one charge puts on another, we say a charge sets up an electric field all around it. The field at a point is the force that a tiny positive test charge would feel there, divided by its charge. For a point charge the field falls off as one over r squared and points radially outward for a positive charge. Then any charge placed there feels a force equal to charge times field.

slides.heading: Field lines of single charges
slides.body_md: A **field line** is a curve whose tangent at each point gives the direction of $\vec E$ there.
bullets: Positive charge: lines point radially **outwards**.
Negative charge: lines point radially **inwards**.
Lines are crowded near the charge, where the field is strong.

visual.alt: Radial field lines pointing inwards to a negative charge

slides.narration: Field lines are a picture of the field. Draw them leaving a positive charge and entering a negative charge. Where lines are close together the field is strong, and where they spread apart it is weak. For a single charge the lines are straight and radial, and the number of lines crossing a sphere round the charge is the same whatever the radius, which matches the inverse square law.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: field of two charges
slides.body_md: Charges $+2.0\,\mu\text{C}$ and $-2.0\,\mu\text{C}$ are $20$ cm apart. Find the field at the midpoint M.
bullets: Step 1 — each charge is $0.10$ m from M: $E_1 = \dfrac{9 \times 10^{9} \times 2.0 \times 10^{-6}}{0.10^2} = 1.8 \times 10^{6}$ N C$^{-1}$.
Step 2 — directions: the field of $+q$ points away from it, towards $-q$; the field of $-q$ points towards $-q$. **Both point the same way.**
Step 3 — add: $E = 2 \times 1.8 \times 10^{6} = 3.6 \times 10^{6}$ N C$^{-1}$, from the positive towards the negative charge.

visual.alt: Field lines of a dipole running from the positive to the negative charge
visual.caption: Traced numerically from Coulomb’s law; arrows checked against the computed field.

slides.narration: At the midpoint each charge is ten centimetres away, so each gives one point eight times ten to the six newtons per coulomb. Now look at directions. The positive charge’s field points away from it, which is towards the negative charge. The negative charge’s field points towards itself. Both are in the same direction, so they add to three point six million newtons per coulomb, pointing from plus to minus.

slides.heading: Field lines of a pair of charges
slides.body_md: For two equal **like** charges the lines bend away from each other. Midway between them the two fields cancel: this is a **neutral point**, where no field line passes.

visual.alt: Field lines of two equal positive charges with a neutral point midway
visual.caption: Traced numerically; no line passes through the neutral point N.

slides.narration: Compare this picture with the dipole on the previous slide. With two equal positive charges, lines from each charge are pushed away from the other, and no line crosses the region between them. Exactly midway the two fields are equal and opposite, so the field is zero. A charge placed at this neutral point feels no force. Far away the pattern looks like that of a single charge of two q.

slides.heading: Properties of electric field lines
slides.body_md: Rules worth memorising for sketches and one-mark questions:
bullets: Start on positive charges and end on negative charges (or go to or come from infinity).
Never cross: at a crossing the field would have two directions at one point.
Electrostatic field lines never form closed loops (the field is conservative).
Crowded lines mean a strong field; evenly spaced parallel lines mean a uniform field.
Lines meet the surface of a conductor at right angles.

rows: Field zero there (for example a neutral point)

slides.narration: Field lines follow a short list of rules. They begin on positive charges and end on negative charges. They never cross, because the field at any point has only one direction. Electrostatic field lines never close on themselves. Their crowding shows the strength of the field, and parallel, equally spaced lines show a uniform field, like the one between two large charged plates.

slides.narration: To sum up: charge is quantised and conserved, and like charges repel. Coulomb’s law gives the force between point charges, weakened in a medium by the dielectric constant. Forces and fields from many charges add as vectors. A point charge has a radial field that falls off as one over r squared, and field lines give a picture of the field’s direction and strength.

slides.heading: Dipoles, flux and Gauss’s law
slides.body_md: Part 2 — a pair of opposite charges, charge spread over lines and surfaces, and a powerful law that turns hard integrals into one-line results.

visual.alt: Flow of the part: dipole, torque, continuous charge, flux, Gauss’s law and its three applications

slides.narration: Many molecules, such as water, behave like a tiny pair of opposite charges called a dipole. We will find the field of a dipole and the turning effect a field has on it, which is how a microwave oven shakes water molecules. Then we move to charge spread over lines and surfaces, define electric flux, and use Gauss’s law to find fields of wires, sheets and shells in a few lines.

slides.heading: The electric dipole
slides.body_md:
Two equal and opposite charges $\pm q$ separated by $2a$ form an **electric dipole**. Its **dipole moment** is
$$\vec p = q \times 2a\,\hat p, \qquad \text{unit C m},$$
directed from $-q$ to $+q$. The total charge is zero, but the field is not.
bullets: Polar molecules (H₂O, HCl) have permanent dipole moments.
Non-polar molecules get an **induced** dipole moment in an external field.
A point dipole: $2a \to 0$, $q \to \infty$ with $p$ fixed.

slides.narration: A dipole is a positive and a negative charge of the same size, held a small distance apart. Its strength is measured by the dipole moment, the charge times the separation, pointing from the negative to the positive charge. Even though the total charge is zero, the two charges are at different places, so their fields do not cancel. Water molecules are natural dipoles, which explains many of water’s properties.

slides.heading: Field of a dipole: axis and equatorial line
slides.body_md: Let the point be at distance $r$ from the centre of the dipole.
columns:
**On the axis** (P)
$$E_\text{axis} = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\,\dfrac{2pr}{(r^2 - a^2)^2} \approx \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\,\dfrac{2p}{r^3}$$
for $r \gg a$; direction **along** $\vec p$.

The nearer charge ($+q$ for P beyond $+q$) gives the larger field.

**On the equatorial line** (Q)
$$E_\text{eq} = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\,\dfrac{p}{(r^2 + a^2)^{3/2}} \approx \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\,\dfrac{p}{r^3}$$
for $r \gg a$; direction **opposite** to $\vec p$.

The components along the bisector cancel; those parallel to the axis add.

slides.narration: On the axis, the two charges are at different distances, so their fields do not cancel. The difference gives two p r over the square of r squared minus a squared, which becomes two p over r cubed far away, along the dipole moment. On the equatorial line, both charges are at the same distance. The sideways parts cancel and the parts parallel to the axis add, giving p over r cubed far away, opposite to the dipole moment.

slides.heading: Deriving the axial field
slides.body_md: At P on the axis, distance $r$ from the centre (beyond $+q$):
bullets: Far away ($r \gg a$): $E \approx \dfrac{2p}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 r^3}$.
The dipole field falls as $1/r^3$, faster than the $1/r^2$ of a single charge.
slides.narration: This derivation is a favourite board question. Write the field of each charge at P with its direction. The positive charge is nearer, so its field is larger and points along the dipole moment. Subtract the two, combine the fractions, and use p equals q times two a. For a far point drop a squared next to r squared. Notice the one over r cubed: the two charges nearly cancel, so the field dies away faster.

slides.heading: Worked example 4: field of a small dipole
slides.body_md: Charges $\pm 2.0$ nC are $4.0$ mm apart. Find the dipole moment and the field $20$ cm from the centre (a) on the axis, (b) on the equatorial line.
bullets: Step 1 — $p = q \times 2a = 2.0 \times 10^{-9} \times 4.0 \times 10^{-3} = 8.0 \times 10^{-12}$ C m.
Step 2 — $r = 0.20$ m $\gg a$, so use the short-dipole results.
Step 3 — axis: $E = \dfrac{2 \times 9 \times 10^{9} \times 8.0 \times 10^{-12}}{0.20^3} = 18$ N C$^{-1}$, along $\vec p$.
Step 4 — equator: $E = \dfrac{9 \times 10^{9} \times 8.0 \times 10^{-12}}{0.20^3} = 9.0$ N C$^{-1}$, opposite to $\vec p$.

visual.alt: Worked table: eighteen newtons per coulomb on the axis along p and nine on the equatorial line opposite to p

slides.narration: First get the dipole moment: two nanocoulombs times four millimetres, which is eight times ten to the minus twelve coulomb metre. Twenty centimetres is fifty times the separation, so the short-dipole formulas are fine. On the axis the field is eighteen newtons per coulomb along p. On the equatorial line it is exactly half, nine, and points the other way. That factor of two is a common one-mark question.

slides.heading: Dipole in a uniform field
slides.body_md:
In a uniform field the forces $+q\vec E$ and $-q\vec E$ are equal and opposite: **net force zero**. They form a couple with torque
$$\vec\tau = \vec p \times \vec E, \qquad \tau = pE\sin\theta$$
bullets: $\theta = 0^\circ$: $\tau = 0$, **stable** equilibrium (p along E).
$\theta = 180^\circ$: $\tau = 0$, **unstable** equilibrium.
$\theta = 90^\circ$: torque is maximum, $pE$.
In a **non-uniform** field there is also a net force.

slides.narration: Put a dipole in a uniform field. The positive end is pushed along the field and the negative end the opposite way, with forces of the same size. So the dipole does not move as a whole, but it turns. The torque is p E sine theta, and it tries to line the dipole up with the field. Aligned with the field it is stable; pointing exactly against the field it is balanced but unstable.

slides.heading: Worked example 5: torque on a dipole
slides.body_md: A dipole of charges $\pm 5.0\,\mu\text{C}$ separated by $2.0$ mm is placed at $30^\circ$ to a uniform field of $2.0 \times 10^{5}$ N C$^{-1}$. Find the torque. At what angle is the torque largest?
bullets: Step 2 — $\tau = pE\sin 30^\circ = 1.0 \times 10^{-8} \times 2.0 \times 10^{5} \times 0.5 = 1.0 \times 10^{-3}$ N m.
Step 3 — largest at $90^\circ$: $\tau_\text{max} = pE = 2.0 \times 10^{-3}$ N m.
Check — the net force is zero because the field is uniform.

slides.heading: Continuous charge distributions
slides.body_md: When charge is spread out, divide it into small elements $dq$, use the point-charge field for each, and add (integrate) the vectors:

visual.alt: Table of linear, surface and volume charge density with their elements and SI units

slides.narration: Real charged objects are not points. Charge on a wire is described by a linear charge density, lambda, in coulombs per metre. Charge on a sheet uses a surface density, sigma, and charge in a volume uses rho. To find the field, split the object into tiny pieces, treat each piece as a point charge, and add all their fields as vectors. For symmetric shapes, Gauss’s law does this much faster.

slides.heading: Setting up the field of a charged line
slides.body_md: Each element $dq = \lambda\,dl$ gives $d\vec E = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\dfrac{\lambda\,dl}{r^2}\hat r$ at P, along the line from the element to P. Different elements give different directions, so add components.

slides.heading: Electric flux
slides.body_md:
Flux measures how much field passes through a surface. For a small area $\Delta \vec S$ (vector normal to the area):
$$\Delta\phi = \vec E \cdot \Delta\vec S = E\,\Delta S\cos\theta, \qquad \phi = \oint \vec E \cdot d\vec S \ \text{(closed surface)}$$
Unit: N m² C$^{-1}$ (or V m). Flux is a **scalar**.
bullets: $\theta = 0^\circ$: flux maximum, $E\Delta S$.
$\theta = 90^\circ$: field along the surface, flux zero.
For a closed surface, outward normals are positive: flux out is positive, flux in is negative.

Flux is the dot product of the field and this area vector, E delta S cos theta. Face the area straight into the field and the flux is largest. Tilt it until the field runs along the surface and the flux is zero. For closed surfaces we always take the outward normal.

slides.heading: Gauss’s law
slides.body_md:
The total flux through **any closed surface** equals the net charge enclosed divided by $\varepsilon_0$:
$$\oint_S \vec E \cdot d\vec S = \dfrac{q_\text{enc}}{\varepsilon_0}$$
bullets: Holds for any shape and size of closed surface.
$\vec E$ on the surface is due to **all** charges, inside and outside; but only enclosed charge gives net flux.
Choose a Gaussian surface through the point where you want $\vec E$, matching the symmetry; it should not pass through a point charge.

slides.narration: The art of Gauss’s law is choosing the surface. For a long straight wire, use a cylinder around it: the field is radial, so only the curved side has flux. For a large flat sheet, use a pillbox crossing the sheet: the field is perpendicular to the sheet, so only the two flat ends have flux. For a spherical shell, use a concentric sphere: the field is radial and the same everywhere on it.

slides.heading: Field of a long wire and of a plane sheet
slides.body_md: Gauss’s law with the surfaces from the previous slide:
columns:
**Infinitely long straight wire** (charge per length $\lambda$), cylinder radius $r$, length $l$:
$$E \cdot 2\pi r l = \dfrac{\lambda l}{\varepsilon_0} \ \Rightarrow\ E = \dfrac{\lambda}{2\pi\varepsilon_0 r}$$
Radially outward for $\lambda > 0$; $E \propto 1/r$.

**Infinite plane sheet** (charge per area $\sigma$), pillbox with end area $A$:
$$2EA = \dfrac{\sigma A}{\varepsilon_0} \ \Rightarrow\ E = \dfrac{\sigma}{2\varepsilon_0}$$
Perpendicular to the sheet, away from it for $\sigma > 0$; **independent of distance**.

visual.alt: Field against distance: a point charge falls as one over r squared, a long wire as one over r, and an infinite sheet stays constant
visual.caption: Same value at r = 1 for comparison.

slides.narration: For the wire, the flux through the curved side is E times two pi r l, and the charge inside is lambda l. So the field is lambda over two pi epsilon nought r, falling as one over r. For the sheet, flux leaves through both ends, two E A, and the charge inside is sigma A. So the field is sigma over two epsilon nought, the same at every distance. The graph compares these with a point charge.

slides.heading: Field of a uniformly charged thin spherical shell
slides.body_md: Shell of radius $R$ and charge $q$ ($\sigma = q/4\pi R^2$). Use a concentric Gaussian sphere of radius $r$:
bullets: **Outside** ($r > R$): $E \cdot 4\pi r^2 = \dfrac{q}{\varepsilon_0}$, so $E = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\dfrac{q}{r^2}$ — as if all the charge were at the centre.
**On the surface** ($r = R$): $E = \dfrac{q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 R^2} = \dfrac{\sigma}{\varepsilon_0}$.
**Inside** ($r < R$): no charge is enclosed, so $E = 0$ everywhere inside.

visual.alt: Graph of field against distance for a charged thin shell: zero for r less than R, jumping to k q over R squared at the surface and then falling as one over r squared
visual.caption: Field of a uniformly charged thin spherical shell of radius R.

slides.narration: For a thin shell, draw a sphere of radius r with the same centre. Outside the shell the sphere encloses all the charge, so the field is exactly that of a point charge at the centre. Inside the shell the sphere encloses no charge, and by symmetry the field must be zero everywhere inside. The graph shows the field jumping from zero to its largest value at the surface and then falling as one over r squared.

slides.heading: Worked example 6: field near a charged wire
slides.body_md: A long straight wire carries $2.0\,\mu\text{C}$ per metre. Find the field $9.0$ cm from it. At what distance is the field half as large?
bullets: Step 1 — $E = \dfrac{\lambda}{2\pi\varepsilon_0 r} = \dfrac{2k\lambda}{r}$, since $\dfrac{1}{2\pi\varepsilon_0} = 2k$.
Step 2 — $E = \dfrac{2 \times 9 \times 10^{9} \times 2.0 \times 10^{-6}}{0.090} = 4.0 \times 10^{5}$ N C$^{-1}$, radially outward.
Step 3 — $E \propto 1/r$, so the field halves at double the distance: **18 cm**.

visual.alt: Field against distance: a point charge falls as one over r squared, a long wire as one over r, and an infinite sheet stays constant
visual.caption: Same value at r = 1 for comparison.

slides.narration: A neat trick: one over two pi epsilon nought equals two k, so you can reuse nine times ten to the nine. Put in two microcoulombs per metre and nine centimetres to get four times ten to the five newtons per coulomb, pointing away from the wire. The field of a wire falls as one over r, not one over r squared, so it halves at twice the distance, eighteen centimetres.

slides.narration: To sum up: a dipole’s field falls as one over r cubed, twice as strong on the axis as on the equatorial line. In a uniform field a dipole feels a torque but no net force. sections.heading: 1. Electric charge and its properties
sections.body_md:
**Electric charge** is a basic property of matter that makes it exert and feel electric forces. SI unit: **coulomb (C)**.

- **Two kinds:** positive and negative. Like charges repel; unlike charges attract. (Glass rubbed with silk becomes positive; the silk negative.)
- **Additivity:** the total charge of a system is the algebraic sum of its charges.
- **Conservation:** the net charge of an isolated system never changes. Charging by rubbing only **transfers electrons**.
- **Quantisation:** $q = n e$, where $n$ is an integer and $e = 1.6 \times 10^{-19}$ C. Everyday charges contain so many $e$ that charge looks continuous.

**Conductors** (metals, the human body, tap water) have free charge carriers; **insulators** (glass, plastic, dry wood) hold charge where it is placed.

**Charging by induction:** bring a charged rod near an insulated conductor; charges separate. Earth the far side, remove the earth connection, then remove the rod. The conductor keeps a charge **opposite** to the rod's. A charged body attracts a neutral light object (a paper bit) because it induces opposite charge on the near side.

key_terms.definition_md: Charge exists only in whole-number multiples of $e = 1.6 \times 10^{-19}$ C.
The total charge of an isolated system stays constant.
Separating charges in a conductor by bringing a charged body near it, without contact.

sections.heading: 2. Coulomb’s law and superposition
sections.body_md:
For two point charges a distance $r$ apart in vacuum:

$$F = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\dfrac{|q_1 q_2|}{r^2},\qquad \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0} = k = 9 \times 10^{9}\ \text{N m}^2\,\text{C}^{-2},\qquad \varepsilon_0 = 8.85 \times 10^{-12}\ \text{C}^2\,\text{N}^{-1}\,\text{m}^{-2}$$

**Vector form:** $\vec F_{21} = k\dfrac{q_1 q_2}{r^2}\hat r_{12}$ (force on $q_2$; $\hat r_{12}$ points from $q_1$ to $q_2$), and $\vec F_{12} = -\vec F_{21}$.

**In a medium** of dielectric constant $\varepsilon_r$: $F = \dfrac{F_\text{vacuum}}{\varepsilon_r}$.

**Superposition:** the force on a charge due to many charges is the **vector sum** of the individual Coulomb forces, each calculated as if the others were absent.

**Method for multi-charge problems:** (1) draw each force with its direction from the signs; (2) find magnitudes; (3) add by components or, for perpendicular forces, by Pythagoras; (4) state magnitude and direction.

*Worked result (deck example 2):* forces of 0.40 N and 0.30 N at right angles give 0.50 N.

key_terms.definition_md: The force between two point charges is proportional to the product of the charges and inversely proportional to the square of their separation.
The factor $\varepsilon_r = \varepsilon/\varepsilon_0$ by which a medium reduces the force between charges.

sections.heading: 4. Electric dipole
sections.body_md:
**Dipole:** charges $+q$ and $-q$ separated by $2a$. **Dipole moment** $\vec p = q(2a)$, from $-q$ to $+q$, unit C m.

| Point at distance $r$ from the centre | Exact | Short dipole ($r \gg a$) | Direction |
|---|---|---|---|
| Axis | $\dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\dfrac{2pr}{(r^2-a^2)^2}$ | $\dfrac{2kp}{r^3}$ | along $\vec p$ |
| Equatorial line | $\dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\dfrac{p}{(r^2+a^2)^{3/2}}$ | $\dfrac{kp}{r^3}$ | opposite to $\vec p$ |

At the same large distance, $E_\text{axis} = 2E_\text{eq}$. A dipole field falls as $1/r^3$.

**Dipole in a uniform field:** net force zero; torque $\vec\tau = \vec p \times \vec E$, $\tau = pE\sin\theta$. Stable equilibrium at $\theta = 0^\circ$, unstable at $180^\circ$, maximum torque $pE$ at $90^\circ$. In a **non-uniform** field there is also a net force (towards stronger field when $\vec p$ is along $\vec E$).

key_terms.definition_md: Product of either charge and the separation, directed from the negative to the positive charge.
A molecule with a permanent dipole moment, such as water.

sections.heading: 6. Electric flux and Gauss’s law
sections.body_md:
**Flux** through a small area: $\Delta\phi = \vec E\cdot\Delta\vec S = E\,\Delta S\cos\theta$, where $\Delta\vec S$ is normal to the area (outward for a closed surface). Unit N m² C$^{-1}$; a scalar.

**Gauss’s law:** $\displaystyle\oint_S \vec E\cdot d\vec S = \dfrac{q_\text{enc}}{\varepsilon_0}$.

- True for any closed surface of any shape.
- $\vec E$ in the integral is the total field (from charges inside and outside), but only enclosed charge contributes net flux.
- Charge outside: net flux zero. Charge inside: flux independent of the surface's size and shape and of where the charge sits inside.
- A charge $q$ at the centre of a cube sends $q/6\varepsilon_0$ through each face.

key_terms.definition_md: The surface integral of the field, $\oint \vec E\cdot d\vec S$; a measure of field lines crossing a surface.
A closed surface chosen to apply Gauss’s law.

sections.heading: 7. Applications of Gauss’s law
sections.body_md:
| Charged object | Gaussian surface | Result |
|---|---|---|
| Infinitely long straight wire, $\lambda$ | Coaxial cylinder; flux only through curved side | $E = \dfrac{\lambda}{2\pi\varepsilon_0 r}$, radial |
| Infinite plane sheet, $\sigma$ | Pillbox; flux only through the two ends | $E = \dfrac{\sigma}{2\varepsilon_0}$, normal, independent of distance |
| Thin spherical shell, $q$, radius $R$, outside ($r > R$) | Concentric sphere | $E = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\dfrac{q}{r^2}$ |
| Same shell, inside ($r < R$) | Concentric sphere, $q_\text{enc} = 0$ | $E = 0$ |

**Steps for a derivation:** draw the Gaussian surface; state why $\vec E$ is constant and normal on part of it and why other parts carry no flux; write flux $=$ charge enclosed $/\varepsilon_0$; solve for $E$; give the direction.

key_terms.definition_md: The field inside a charged conducting or thin shell is zero, so the inside is screened from charges on the shell.

notes.exam_tips_md:
- **Units first:** $\mu$C $= 10^{-6}$ C, nC $= 10^{-9}$ C, cm $= 10^{-2}$ m.
- **Direction always:** a force or field answer without a direction loses a mark.
- **Derivations** (dipole axial or equatorial field, wire, sheet, shell): figure, directions, the key step, the final result, the approximation used.
- **Gauss's law:** name the surface and justify where the flux is zero.
- **Field lines:** arrows on every line, no crossings, density shows strength.

cards.front_md: Charge on an electron?
cards.back_md: $-1.6 \times 10^{-19}$ C (magnitude $e$).

cards.front_md: Quantisation of charge?
cards.back_md: Any charge is $q = n e$ with $n$ an integer.

cards.front_md: Conservation of charge?
cards.back_md: The net charge of an isolated system stays constant; charge is only transferred.

cards.front_md: A rod becomes positive on rubbing. What moved?
cards.back_md: Electrons moved **off** the rod; protons do not move.

cards.front_md: Why does a charged comb pick up paper bits?
cards.back_md: It induces opposite charge on the near side of the paper; attraction to the nearer charge wins.

cards.front_md: Charging by induction: sign of charge left on the conductor?
cards.back_md: Opposite to the charge on the inducing rod.

cards.front_md: Coulomb’s law?
cards.back_md: $F = k\dfrac{|q_1q_2|}{r^2}$, along the line joining the charges.

cards.front_md: Value of $k = 1/4\pi\varepsilon_0$?
Value of $\varepsilon_0$?
Force between charges in a medium of dielectric constant $\varepsilon_r$?
cards.back_md: Vacuum force divided by $\varepsilon_r$.

cards.front_md: Principle of superposition?
cards.back_md: The net force (or field) is the vector sum of the forces (fields) due to each charge alone.

cards.front_md: Define electric field.
cards.back_md: Force per unit small positive test charge: $\vec E = \vec F/q_0$, unit N C$^{-1}$.

cards.front_md: Field of a point charge?
cards.back_md: $E = kq/r^2$, radial (outward for $+q$).

cards.front_md: Why can field lines never cross?
cards.back_md: The field would have two directions at the crossing point.

cards.front_md: Why are electrostatic field lines never closed loops?
cards.back_md: They start on $+$ and end on $-$ charges; the electrostatic field is conservative.

cards.front_md: Neutral point between two equal like charges?
cards.back_md: Midway between them.

cards.front_md: Dipole moment: definition and direction?
cards.back_md: $p = q \times 2a$, from $-q$ to $+q$; unit C m.

cards.front_md: Short-dipole field on the axis?
cards.back_md: $2kp/r^3$, along $\vec p$.

cards.front_md: Short-dipole field on the equatorial line?
cards.back_md: $kp/r^3$, opposite to $\vec p$.

cards.front_md: Torque on a dipole in a uniform field?
cards.back_md: $\vec\tau = \vec p \times \vec E$, $\tau = pE\sin\theta$; net force zero.

cards.front_md: Stable and unstable positions of a dipole?
cards.back_md: Stable: $\vec p$ along $\vec E$ ($0^\circ$). Unstable: opposite ($180^\circ$).

cards.front_md: How does a dipole field fall with distance?
Linear, surface, volume charge densities?
Electric flux through an area?
cards.back_md: $\phi = \vec E\cdot\vec S = ES\cos\theta$; unit N m² C$^{-1}$.

cards.front_md: Gauss’s law?
cards.back_md: Total flux through a closed surface $= q_\text{enc}/\varepsilon_0$.

cards.front_md: Flux through a closed surface with a charge outside it?
cards.back_md: Zero.

cards.front_md: Charge $q$ at the centre of a cube: flux through one face?
cards.back_md: $q/6\varepsilon_0$.

cards.front_md: Field of an infinitely long wire?
cards.back_md: $\lambda/2\pi\varepsilon_0 r$, radial.

cards.front_md: Field of an infinite plane sheet?
cards.back_md: $\sigma/2\varepsilon_0$, independent of distance.

cards.front_md: Field inside and outside a thin charged shell?
cards.back_md: Inside 0; outside $kq/r^2$ as if the charge were at the centre.

cards.front_md: Gaussian surface for a long wire?
cards.back_md: A coaxial cylinder; flux only through its curved surface.

cards.front_md: Exam tip: Gauss’s law derivations?
cards.back_md: Name the surface, explain zero-flux parts, write flux $= q_\text{enc}/\varepsilon_0$, solve, give direction.

questions.stem_md: In an oil-drop experiment, which of the following could be the charge on a drop?
questions.solution_md: A charge must be $n e$. $\dfrac{4.8 \times 10^{-19}}{1.6 \times 10^{-19}} = 3$, a whole number; the others give 1.5, 0.625 and 3.5 — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Two point charges exert a force $F$ on each other. Both charges are doubled and the distance between them is also doubled. The new force is
questions.solution_md: $F \propto q_1q_2/r^2$: the product of charges becomes 4 times and $r^2$ becomes 4 times, so the force is unchanged — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Two small charged spheres repel each other with a force of 0.4 N in air. With the same separation in a liquid, the force is 0.05 N. The dielectric constant of the liquid is
questions.solution_md: $\varepsilon_r = F_\text{air}/F_\text{liquid} = 0.4/0.05 = 8$ — option (d).

questions.stem_md: A plastic comb gains $2.5 \times 10^{13}$ electrons when it is run through dry hair. The charge on the comb is
questions.solution_md: $q = n e = 2.5 \times 10^{13} \times 1.6 \times 10^{-19} = 4.0 \times 10^{-6}$ C, negative because electrons were gained — option (d).

questions.stem_md: Two identical metal spheres carry $+6\,\mu\text{C}$ and $-2\,\mu\text{C}$. They are touched together and then separated. The charge on each is
questions.solution_md: Total charge is conserved: $+6 - 2 = +4\,\mu\text{C}$, shared equally by identical spheres, so $+2\,\mu\text{C}$ each — option (d).

questions.stem_md: A positively charged rod is held near an insulated, uncharged metal sphere. The sphere is touched with an earthed wire, the wire is removed, and then the rod is taken away. The sphere is now

options.text_md: positive on one side and negative on the other

questions.solution_md: The rod pulls electrons from earth onto the sphere while it is earthed; they are trapped when the wire is removed first — option (b).

questions.stem_md: In $\vec F_{21} = k\dfrac{q_1q_2}{r^2}\hat r_{12}$, $\hat r_{12}$ points from $q_1$ to $q_2$. If $q_1 > 0$ and $q_2 < 0$, the force on $q_2$

options.text_md: is perpendicular to the line joining them

questions.solution_md: $q_1q_2 < 0$, so $\vec F_{21}$ is along $-\hat r_{12}$, i.e. towards $q_1$: attraction — option (c).

questions.stem_md: Two protons are a distance $r$ apart. The ratio of the electric force to the gravitational force between them is about ($G = 6.67 \times 10^{-11}$ N m² kg$^{-2}$, $m_p = 1.67 \times 10^{-27}$ kg)
questions.solution_md: $\dfrac{F_e}{F_g} = \dfrac{ke^2}{Gm_p^2} = \dfrac{9 \times 10^{9} \times (1.6 \times 10^{-19})^2}{6.67 \times 10^{-11} \times (1.67 \times 10^{-27})^2} \approx 1.2 \times 10^{36}$; $r$ cancels — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Charges $+q$ and $+4q$ are fixed a distance $d$ apart. Where should a third charge be placed so that the net force on it is zero?
questions.solution_md: At distance $x$ from $+q$: $\dfrac{q}{x^2} = \dfrac{4q}{(d-x)^2}$, so $d - x = 2x$ and $x = d/3$; between like charges the two forces are opposite — option (c).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A charged balloon attracts small uncharged bits of paper.

**Reason (R):** The balloon induces charges on the paper, and the induced charge nearer the balloon is opposite in sign to the balloon’s charge.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: Both are true. The opposite induced charge is nearer, so its attraction beats the repulsion of the farther like charge; R explains A — option (a).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A body can carry a charge of $2.4 \times 10^{-19}$ C.

**Reason (R):** Electric charge is quantised.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: R is true. A is false: $\dfrac{2.4 \times 10^{-19}}{1.6 \times 10^{-19}} = 1.5$ is not a whole number — option (d).

questions.stem_md: True or false? When a glass rod is rubbed with silk, protons move from the silk to the glass.
questions.solution_md: False. Electrons move from the glass to the silk; protons stay in the nuclei. The glass becomes positive because it loses electrons.

questions.stem_md: The charge on any body is a whole-number multiple of the charge of an ___.
questions.solution_md: Of an **electron** (magnitude $e = 1.6 \times 10^{-19}$ C), the basic unit of charge.

questions.stem_md: Two identical small metal spheres with charges $+6\,\mu\text{C}$ and $-2\,\mu\text{C}$ attract each other with a force $F$ when a distance $r$ apart. They are touched and returned to the same separation. Find the ratio (new force)/(old force), to two decimal places.
questions.solution_md: After touching each has $+2\,\mu\text{C}$. $F \propto |q_1q_2|$: old product $6 \times 2 = 12$, new product $2 \times 2 = 4$. Ratio $= 4/12 \approx 0.33$ (now repulsive).

questions.stem_md: Charges $+4\,\mu\text{C}$, $+1\,\mu\text{C}$ and $-2\,\mu\text{C}$ are fixed on the x-axis at $x = 0$, $x = 0.20$ m and $x = 0.50$ m. Find the magnitude of the net force on the $+1\,\mu\text{C}$ charge, in newtons.
questions.solution_md: From $+4\,\mu\text{C}$ (repulsion, $+x$): $\dfrac{9 \times 10^{9} \times 4 \times 10^{-6} \times 1 \times 10^{-6}}{0.20^2} = 0.90$ N. From $-2\,\mu\text{C}$ (attraction, $+x$): $\dfrac{9 \times 10^{9} \times 2 \times 10^{-6} \times 1 \times 10^{-6}}{0.30^2} = 0.20$ N. Both along $+x$: $0.90 + 0.20 = 1.1$ N.

questions.stem_md: An electron is released from rest in a uniform field of $2.0 \times 10^{4}$ N C$^{-1}$ that points to the right. Its acceleration is ($m_e = 9.1 \times 10^{-31}$ kg)
questions.solution_md: $a = \dfrac{eE}{m_e} = \dfrac{1.6 \times 10^{-19} \times 2.0 \times 10^{4}}{9.1 \times 10^{-31}} \approx 3.5 \times 10^{15}$ m s$^{-2}$, opposite to $\vec E$ since the charge is negative — option (d). (The third value uses the proton mass.)

questions.stem_md: True or false? Two electric field lines can cross each other at a point where the field is very strong.
questions.solution_md: False. At a crossing the tangent, and so the field, would have two directions at one point, which is impossible. A strong field is shown by crowded lines, not by crossings.

questions.stem_md: Which statement about electrostatic field lines is NOT correct?

options.text_md: They start on positive charges and end on negative charges
Their tangent gives the direction of the field
They form closed loops around charges
They are closer together where the field is stronger

questions.solution_md: Electrostatic field lines begin and end on charges and never close on themselves — option (c).

questions.stem_md: Charges $+4q$ and $-q$ are fixed a distance $d$ apart. The point where the electric field is zero lies

options.text_md: on the line, a distance $d$ beyond $-q$ (away from $+4q$)
on the line, a distance $d$ beyond $+4q$

questions.solution_md: Between unlike charges both fields point the same way, so the zero lies outside, near the smaller charge. At $x$ beyond $-q$: $\dfrac{4q}{(d+x)^2} = \dfrac{q}{x^2}$, so $d + x = 2x$, $x = d$ — option (c).

questions.stem_md: In a field-line diagram, lines are closely packed near point A and widely spaced near point B. Which is correct?

options.text_md: The field is stronger at A than at B
The field is stronger at B than at A
The field is zero at B
A charge at A feels no force

questions.solution_md: The density of field lines shows the field strength — option (a).

questions.stem_md: The test charge used to define the electric field at a point is taken to be very small because

options.text_md: a small charge feels a larger force
the field depends on the size of the test charge
a large test charge would disturb the charges that produce the field
only small charges obey Coulomb’s law

questions.solution_md: A tiny test charge measures the field without moving the source charges — option (c).

questions.stem_md: Find the magnitude of the electric field 30 cm from a point charge of 5.0 nC in air, in N C⁻¹.
Charges of +3.0 nC and +1.0 nC are 20 cm apart in air. Find the magnitude of the electric field at the midpoint between them, in N C⁻¹.
questions.solution_md: Each is $0.10$ m away. $E_1 = \dfrac{9 \times 10^{9} \times 3.0 \times 10^{-9}}{0.10^2} = 2700$ N C$^{-1}$ (away from the 3 nC charge); $E_2 = 900$ N C$^{-1}$ (away from the 1 nC charge). Opposite directions: $2700 - 900 = 1800$ N C$^{-1}$, towards the 1 nC charge.

marking_scheme.step: 1800 N C⁻¹ towards the 1 nC charge

questions.stem_md: The SI unit of electric field is newton per ___.
questions.solution_md: Newton per **coulomb** (N C$^{-1}$), the force per unit charge; it is the same as volt per metre.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Electric field lines in a charge-free region are continuous curves.

**Reason (R):** Two electric field lines can never cross each other.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: Both are true. Continuity follows because lines only begin or end on charges; R is a separate property (one direction at each point) and does not explain A — option (b).

questions.stem_md: The field at a point on the axis of a short dipole, a distance $r$ from its centre, is $E$. The field at a point on its equatorial line at a distance $2r$ is
questions.solution_md: $E = 2kp/r^3$. At $2r$ on the equator: $\dfrac{kp}{(2r)^3} = \dfrac{kp}{8r^3} = \dfrac{1}{16}\cdot\dfrac{2kp}{r^3}$ — option (b).

questions.stem_md: The electric field at a point on the equatorial line of a dipole is directed

options.text_md: along the equatorial line, away from the dipole
along the equatorial line, towards the dipole

Swapping the labels gives $\vec F_{12} = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\dfrac{q_1q_2}{r^2}\hat r_{21}$, and $\hat r_{21} = -\hat r_{12}$. answer.model_answer_md: The forces on the charges are $+q\vec E$ and $-q\vec E$: equal and opposite, so the **net force is zero**. They form a couple, $\tau = pE\sin\theta$. The dipole is in **stable equilibrium** when $\vec p$ is **along** $\vec E$ ($\theta = 0$); a small twist produces a torque that turns it back.

answer.model_answer_md: Each sheet gives $\dfrac{\sigma}{2\varepsilon_0}$, away from $+\sigma$ and towards $-\sigma$. (a) **Between**, both point from the positive to the negative sheet: $E = \dfrac{\sigma}{2\varepsilon_0} + \dfrac{\sigma}{2\varepsilon_0} = \dfrac{\sigma}{\varepsilon_0}$. (b) **Outside**, they point in opposite directions and cancel: $E = 0$.

answer.model_answer_md: Each pair: $F = \dfrac{9 \times 10^{9} \times (1.0 \times 10^{-6})^2}{0.10^2} = 0.90$ N, repulsive. The two forces on one charge make $60^\circ$ with each other. Resultant $= 2F\cos 30^\circ = \sqrt{3}F \approx 1.56$ N, along the bisector of the angle at that corner, **pointing away** from the triangle (away from the opposite side’s midpoint).

answer.model_answer_md: Between **like** charges the two fields point in opposite directions, so they can cancel there; outside they point the same way. At distance $x$ from the $9\,\mu\text{C}$ charge: $\dfrac{9}{x^2} = \dfrac{1}{(0.40 - x)^2}$, so $3(0.40 - x) = x$ and $x = 0.30$ m. The neutral point is **30 cm from the 9 μC charge** (10 cm from the 1 μC charge).

questions.stem_md: Derive an expression for the electric field at a point on the equatorial line of an electric dipole, a distance $r$ from its centre. Write its form when $r \gg a$.

answer.model_answer_md:
Each charge is at distance $\sqrt{r^2 + a^2}$, so $|\vec E_{+}| = |\vec E_{-}| = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\dfrac{q}{r^2 + a^2}$. Their components **along the equatorial line cancel**; the components **parallel to the axis** add, each being $E_{+}\cos\theta$ with $\cos\theta = \dfrac{a}{\sqrt{r^2 + a^2}}$:
$$E = 2 \cdot \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\dfrac{q}{r^2+a^2}\cdot\dfrac{a}{\sqrt{r^2+a^2}} = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\dfrac{p}{(r^2+a^2)^{3/2}}$$
directed **opposite to $\vec p$**. For $r \gg a$: $E \approx \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\dfrac{p}{r^3}$.

questions.solution_md: Resolve both fields; perpendicular parts cancel, axial parts add.

marking_scheme.step: Equal magnitudes and resolution with cos θ = a/√(r² + a²)
E = p/[4πε₀(r² + a²)^{3/2}], opposite to p

questions.stem_md: Use Gauss’s law to derive the electric field at a distance $r$ from an infinitely long straight wire with uniform linear charge density $\lambda$.

answer.model_answer_md: By symmetry the field is **radial** and has the same size at all points a distance $r$ from the wire. Take a **coaxial cylinder** of radius $r$ and length $l$. On the flat ends $\vec E$ is parallel to the surface, so their flux is **zero**. On the curved surface $\vec E$ is along $d\vec S$ and constant: flux $= E \cdot 2\pi r l$. Charge enclosed $= \lambda l$. Gauss’s law: $E \cdot 2\pi r l = \dfrac{\lambda l}{\varepsilon_0}$, so $E = \dfrac{\lambda}{2\pi\varepsilon_0 r}$, radially outward for $\lambda > 0$.

questions.solution_md: Coaxial cylinder; only the curved surface carries flux.

marking_scheme.step: Gaussian cylinder and zero flux through the ends

questions.stem_md: An electron is in a uniform field of $5.0 \times 10^{4}$ N C$^{-1}$. Find (a) the force on it and (b) its acceleration. (c) Explain why its weight can be ignored. ($m_e = 9.1 \times 10^{-31}$ kg, $g = 9.8$ m s$^{-2}$.)

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) $F = eE = 1.6 \times 10^{-19} \times 5.0 \times 10^{4} = 8.0 \times 10^{-15}$ N, opposite to $\vec E$.
(b) $a = \dfrac{F}{m_e} = \dfrac{8.0 \times 10^{-15}}{9.1 \times 10^{-31}} \approx 8.8 \times 10^{15}$ m s$^{-2}$.
(c) Its weight is $m_e g \approx 8.9 \times 10^{-30}$ N, about $10^{15}$ times smaller than the electric force, so it has no noticeable effect.

questions.solution_md: F = eE, a = F/m; compare with mg.

marking_scheme.step: Weight about 10¹⁵ times smaller than F, negligible

questions.stem_md: Derive an expression for the electric field at a point on the axis of an electric dipole at a distance $r$ from its centre. Show that for $r \gg a$ it varies as $1/r^3$, and compare it with the field at the same distance on the equatorial line.

answer.model_answer_md:
Let $-q$ be at A and $+q$ at B, with $AB = 2a$ and P on the axis beyond B at distance $r$ from the centre O.

Field due to $+q$ (distance $r - a$): $E_{+} = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\dfrac{q}{(r-a)^2}$, along $\vec p$.
Field due to $-q$ (distance $r + a$): $E_{-} = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\dfrac{q}{(r+a)^2}$, opposite to $\vec p$.

Since $E_{+} > E_{-}$, the net field is along $\vec p$:
$$E = \dfrac{q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\left[\dfrac{1}{(r-a)^2} - \dfrac{1}{(r+a)^2}\right] = \dfrac{q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\dfrac{4ar}{(r^2-a^2)^2} = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\dfrac{2pr}{(r^2-a^2)^2}$$
using $p = 2qa$. For $r \gg a$, $r^2 - a^2 \approx r^2$, so $E \approx \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\dfrac{2p}{r^3}$: it varies as $1/r^3$.

On the equatorial line at the same distance, $E_\text{eq} \approx \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\dfrac{p}{r^3}$, opposite to $\vec p$. So $E_\text{axis} = 2E_\text{eq}$, and the two fields are in opposite directions.

questions.solution_md: Subtract the fields of the two charges at P, simplify, then approximate for a far point.

marking_scheme.step: Labelled figure and the two fields with directions

questions.stem_md: (a) State Gauss’s law in electrostatics. (b) Use it to derive the electric field due to an infinite plane sheet with uniform surface charge density $\sigma$. (c) A large sheet produces a field of $3.0 \times 10^{3}$ N C$^{-1}$. Find $\sigma$.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) The total electric flux through any closed surface equals $\dfrac{1}{\varepsilon_0}$ times the net charge enclosed: $\oint \vec E\cdot d\vec S = \dfrac{q_\text{enc}}{\varepsilon_0}$.

(b) By symmetry, $\vec E$ is **perpendicular** to the sheet, pointing away on both sides (for $\sigma > 0$), with the same size at equal distances. Take a **cylindrical pillbox** crossing the sheet, end faces of area $A$ parallel to it. On the curved side $\vec E$ is parallel to the surface: **no flux**. Through each end, flux $= EA$. Total flux $= 2EA$; charge enclosed $= \sigma A$. So $2EA = \dfrac{\sigma A}{\varepsilon_0}$ and $E = \dfrac{\sigma}{2\varepsilon_0}$, independent of distance.

(c) $\sigma = 2\varepsilon_0 E = 2 \times 8.85 \times 10^{-12} \times 3.0 \times 10^{3} = 5.31 \times 10^{-8}$ C m$^{-2}$.

questions.solution_md: Pillbox Gaussian surface; flux only through the two ends; then rearrange for σ.

marking_scheme.step: Pillbox and zero flux through the curved side

questions.stem_md: A thin spherical shell of radius $R$ carries charge $q$ spread uniformly. (a) Use Gauss’s law to find the field at a distance $r$ from the centre for $r > R$ and for $r < R$. (b) Sketch a graph of $E$ against $r$. (c) For $q = 4.0$ nC and $R = 20$ cm, find the field at the surface and at 40 cm from the centre.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) By symmetry $\vec E$ is radial and has the same size everywhere on a concentric sphere of radius $r$.
**Outside** ($r > R$): the Gaussian sphere encloses $q$, so $E \cdot 4\pi r^2 = \dfrac{q}{\varepsilon_0}$, giving $E = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\dfrac{q}{r^2}$ — as if all the charge were at the centre.
**Inside** ($r < R$): the sphere encloses no charge, so $E \cdot 4\pi r^2 = 0$ and $E = 0$.

(b) $E$ is zero from $r = 0$ to $r = R$, jumps to its largest value $\dfrac{q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 R^2}$ at $r = R$, and then falls as $1/r^2$.

(c) At the surface: $E = \dfrac{9 \times 10^{9} \times 4.0 \times 10^{-9}}{0.20^2} = 900$ N C$^{-1}$. At 40 cm: $E = \dfrac{9 \times 10^{9} \times 4.0 \times 10^{-9}}{0.40^2} = 225$ N C$^{-1}$ (one quarter, since the distance is doubled).

questions.solution_md: Concentric Gaussian spheres outside and inside; then substitute.

questions.stem_md: (a) State the principle of superposition for electrostatic forces. (b) Equal charges of $+1.0\,\mu$C are placed at the four corners A, B, C and D of a square of side 10 cm. Find the magnitude and direction of the net force on the charge at D.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) The force on a charge due to a group of charges is the **vector sum** of the forces each charge would exert on it alone; each pair force is unaffected by the others.

(b) Charges at A and C are adjacent to D ($r = 0.10$ m): each force $= \dfrac{9 \times 10^{9} \times (1.0 \times 10^{-6})^2}{0.10^2} = 0.90$ N, repulsive, along AD and CD extended, at $90^\circ$ to each other. Their resultant $= \sqrt{2} \times 0.90 \approx 1.27$ N, along the diagonal BD, away from B.
The charge at B is $0.10\sqrt{2}$ m away: force $= \dfrac{9 \times 10^{9} \times (1.0 \times 10^{-6})^2}{0.020} = 0.45$ N, also along BD, away from B.
Net force $= 1.27 + 0.45 \approx 1.72$ N, along the diagonal from B through D, pointing **away from the centre** of the square.

questions.solution_md: Add the two perpendicular adjacent forces, then add the diagonal force along the same line.

marking_scheme.step: Net ≈ 1.72 N away from the centre

questions.stem_md: (a) Show that a dipole of moment $\vec p$ in a uniform field $\vec E$ experiences a torque $\vec\tau = \vec p \times \vec E$ and no net force. (b) A dipole of moment $3.0 \times 10^{-9}$ C m is placed in a field of $2.0 \times 10^{4}$ N C$^{-1}$. Find the torque when $\vec p$ is at $30^\circ$ and at $90^\circ$ to $\vec E$. (c) In which orientation is the dipole in unstable equilibrium?

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) The forces on $+q$ and $-q$ are $+q\vec E$ and $-q\vec E$. Their sum is zero, so **no net force**. They act along parallel lines separated by $2a\sin\theta$, forming a couple: $\tau = qE \times 2a\sin\theta = pE\sin\theta$. The torque tends to turn $\vec p$ towards $\vec E$; in vector form $\vec\tau = \vec p \times \vec E$.

(b) At $30^\circ$: $\tau = 3.0 \times 10^{-9} \times 2.0 \times 10^{4} \times 0.5 = 3.0 \times 10^{-5}$ N m. At $90^\circ$: $\tau = pE = 6.0 \times 10^{-5}$ N m (the maximum).

(c) **Unstable** when $\vec p$ is **antiparallel** to $\vec E$ ($\theta = 180^\circ$): the torque is zero, but any small turn produces a torque that turns it further away.

questions.solution_md: Couple of forces ±qE with arm 2a sin θ; then substitute.

questions.passage_md: In some industrial inkjet printers that print dates on food packets, tiny ink drops are given a small negative charge and then pass between two parallel plates. The upper plate is positive and the lower plate negative, so there is a nearly uniform field between them. By changing the charge on each drop, the printer steers it to the right spot on the packet.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** (a) Upwards, towards the positive plate

**(b)** 0.2 μN

**(c)** (i) The force is $qE$, so the drop with **twice the charge** feels twice the force and twice the **acceleration** ($a = qE/m$). It spends the same time between the plates, so its sideways deflection ($\tfrac{1}{2}at^2$) is **twice as large**.

**OR** (ii) Each large plate acts like a plane sheet whose field $\sigma/2\varepsilon_0$ does **not depend on distance**. Between the plates the two fields point the same way and add to $\sigma/\varepsilon_0$, the **same at every point**. Only near the edges, where the plates stop looking infinite, does the field bend.

questions.solution_md:
**(a)** The field points from the positive (upper) plate to the negative (lower) plate, i.e. downwards; a negative charge is pushed opposite to the field — option (a).

**(b)** $F = qE = 2.0 \times 10^{-13} \times 1.0 \times 10^{6} = 2.0 \times 10^{-7}$ N. In μN: $2.0 \times 10^{-7} \times 10^{6} = 0.20$.
